candidates.title: What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement
candidates.abstract: Weight-space programming (WSP) lets a language model construct executable weight updates for another network. We study diffusion concept editing through an interface in which programs define training contexts, preservation constraints and update directions, while a shared numerical fitter selects their coefficients. We compare generated programs with published editors, a shared-panel hand-written baseline and budget-matched search over conventional edits on 24 TIMED test edits for Stable Diffusion 1.4. The preregistered rewrite pipeline shows no advantage over the strong baseline. In an exploratory comparison, one-shot Astra programs improve fresh-scene VLM joint success, which requires subject presence together with whole-image target matching, by +10.0 points over the shared-panel baseline, while CLIP relative match shows no detectable change. These programs organise adjustable directions around protected text-state subspaces. Probing and rewriting the Astra programs then raises CLIP by +6.2 points while joint success changes by -9.7. On a fixed 144-image sample, five additional evaluators give point estimates in the same directions under whole-image target matching; checks of subject-local change give less decisive differences. Together, these results identify useful behaviour in complete generated programs and show that score-guided revision need not preserve it: program construction and revision should be evaluated as distinct stages of a WSP pipeline.

candidates.title: Weight-Space Programming Doesn't Need Transformers
candidates.abstract: Standard neural architectures such as the Transformer were chosen because they train well with gradient descent and run fast on GPUs. In weight-space programming, a large language model (LLM) writes target weights by hand without gradient-based training, so those reasons no longer apply. Should we keep the Transformer? Given minimal guidance, ten labeled examples, and a sandbox, mainly on multiple-choice questions, we task three frontier LLMs with either generating the weights of a fixed architecture or designing the architecture themselves. When free to design, all three compile plain-text facts into a sparse table queried by a fixed procedure, reaching up to 54.4% test accuracy. An LLM-designed model achieves higher test accuracy than the most accurate released Transformer that the same LLM wrote while using about 1,800x fewer parameters. Without gradients, they choose a table, in which the LLM can state what each weight means and can find and rewrite a wrong one. Each wrong answer points to one row, and removing a row changes about one other answer. From this, we propose an associative-memory-based model up to 17x faster on GPUs than a same-sized Transformer. We also test pretrained weights, other benchmarks, and tasks where models generate answers. Pretrained LLMs remain more accurate; the claim concerns which structure to build when writing weights.

candidates.title: Weight-Space Programming for Materials Science
candidates.abstract: A materials discovery campaign often begins with almost no measurements of the property it is searching for, and the models that rank candidates or screen the output of a generator then have to be built from those first few labels. Following recent work on weight-space programming, in which a language model writes the weights of a small network directly as text, we show that a general-purpose model, given the task in words, the names of the inputs and a network of 16 hidden units with every weight set to zero, can provide this starting point by filling in all of the weights from what it has learned about materials. With no labels, the networks of the strongest model rank experimental alloys at Spearman co-efficient = 0.64 to 0.79, where the best of five simple descriptors reaches 0.47 to 0.62. They rank the bulk modulus of crystals added during generative discovery loops at 0.95, where the inverse volume per atom reaches 0.89, and 35 phase-equilibrium targets computed with Thermo-Calc at a mean of 0.67, close to the 0.70 of an extrapolation from calculated binary and ternary data. As the prior mean of a Gaussian process they raise the ranking at five labels from 0.35 to 0.69 on alloys and from 0.15 to 0.95 on crystals, and they lower the regret of Bayesian optimization significantly on 4 of 5 experimental tasks and on 13 to 16 of 33 computed targets, depending on how multiple tests are corrected, without raising it significantly on any. The same networks also serve as the mean of a Bayesian neural network and as a screen for the samples of two crystal generators, where they do as well as standard models trained on 400 labeled structures. The gain is confined to the first tens of labels and to targets that no rule or sub-system extrapolation already ranks.

candidates.title: Can Weight-Space Programming Alter Learned Ethical Priorities?
candidates.abstract: We investigate whether a weight edit can alter how a model trades off honoring a commitment against benefiting more people. In a concept-supervised text model, we alter fitted choice weights so that the benefit required to override a formal pledge is larger than for an ordinary promise. Across six independently trained text readers, the edit selects the larger group in both orders on 100% of targeted ordinary conflicts and 83.3% of targeted formal conflicts. It preserves the source model's success rates on smaller conflicts and its factual accuracy. The remaining formal-conflict failures coincide with errors reading a beneficiary number. A separate classifier demonstrates why this distinction matters: reusing a factual answer passes an unconditional choice test but fails to preserve small-gap promises. In a YOLO11n pilot on COCO128, a bias edit increased small-target matches from 3/43 to 9/43, and an equivalent score calibration reproduced the retained detections. These exploratory results show a way to test selective changes to learned priorities in a model with an exposed trade-off mechanism. Whether the method can discover such changes in less structured language models remains open.

candidates.title: SheetAlign: Grounded Interaction and Stage-Isolated Learning for Spreadsheet Agents
candidates.abstract: Spreadsheets are widely used for data analysis and supporting decision-making. Automating spreadsheet analysis while protecting sensitive data and controlling deployment costs motivates locally deployed open-weight large language models (LLMs). Meanwhile, complex spreadsheet tasks require both task reasoning and workbook understanding, while predefined operation interfaces impose additional tool-selection and invocation demands. We introduce SheetAlign, a spreadsheet manipulation framework with stage-isolated policy learning, organized around where to operate, what to change, and how to implement transformations. Task-guided inspection and API grounding anchor code generation in workbook observations and available operations, while stage-isolated learning optimizes program generation and review using edit-progress rewards. At inference, execution consistency selects programs through agreement among workbook states. On SpreadsheetBench, our grounded task interface improves Qwen3-4B's accuracy from 13.5% to 29.2% on average without training. With learning and execution consistency, SheetAlign achieves 32.8% accuracy on average on SpreadsheetBench and 30.1% on Domain-Spreadsheet, outperforming comparable baselines. The code will be made publicly available upon publication.

candidates.title: Weight-Space Programming Writes In-Context Learning and Matches Fine-Tuning in Language Models
candidates.abstract: Weight-space programming is a frontier language model's recently reported ability to read and rewrite another network's weights without gradient descent. We investigate how examples can provide a weight update so that a weaker language model performs the task with nothing in the prompt, and study what it edits. Our experiments cover six tasks, four frontier editors and three families of weaker language models, without the editors being told anything about in-context learning (ICL). In most runs, the few-shot minus zero-shot residual is measured at the final prompt token, the ICL task vector, and write it into the weights, at its sparsest into near-silent MLP units keyed to the prompt format. Results reach the accuracy of ICL and of fine-tuning on the same examples, LoRA included, usually leaving perplexity untouched, with worse performance under changes of wording. We also qualify the comparison by counting unfinished runs, observing that one editor falls below fine-tuning; held only to the seen examples, without task pairs of their own, only the strongest editor has similar performance. Given a task and unlabelled inputs, that editor writes its own examples and does nearly as well on unseen items as with labels.

candidates.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming
candidates.abstract: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp

candidates.title: WeightCode: Installing New Capabilities into Neural Networks via Weight-Space Programming
candidates.abstract: Neural networks encode learned capabilities in their weights, yet extending those capabilities with explicit task knowledge remains a fundamental challenge. Here we show that Weight-Space Programming (WSP), in which executable programs read, construct or modify a network's weights directly, can install new capabilities within trained neural networks. WeightCode, a WSP framework, uses a frozen language model to write executable weight programs that install new computations into trained neural networks using task knowledge and their existing weights, without gradient-based training. Once installed, the new capabilities run independently of the language model. Given a grammar or eight demonstrations, weight programs enable previously unseen command compositions (0% to 99.8% exact match) and a new pickup action (0% to 98.4% success), while preserving the original command and navigation capabilities. On ImageNet, four weight programs achieve net gains of 8.84-17.62 points while preserving clean accuracy, outperforming the best of eight fine-tuning methods under matched examples, checks, and retention constraints. In a Vision Transformer, causal interventions show that installed noise-correction gates drive robustness gains, while their selective activation preserves clean accuracy. Rerun on five independently trained Vision Transformers without further language model calls, ten weight programs retain 83-110% of their source-network gains on average, whereas copying their fixed weight edits yields negligible gains. Six programs written for an already edited network add 5.23-14.50 points of contrast robustness while retaining the previously installed noise gain. Together, these results establish WSP as a new route to acquiring and accumulating capabilities in trained neural networks through reusable weight programs.

candidates.title: Loop-OPF: Solver-Informed Learning for Optimal Power Flow with Inference-Time Topology Adaptivity
candidates.abstract: Learning for optimal power flow (OPF) has recently been advocated to accelerate OPF solutions by using a pre-trained neural network (NN) to predict directly from given inputs such as the load demand. However, existing learning-for-OPF methods largely fall short of ensuring the optimality and feasibility of their predictions. They also struggle to adapt at inference time to unseen topology scenarios, such as those caused by line or generator outages. This work puts forth Loop-OPF, a solver-informed NN that builds its layers from the iterations of the primal-dual hybrid gradient (PDHG) method. Under standard convexity and regularity conditions on DC-OPF, the resultant fixed-point output of Loop-OPF is thus optimal and feasible. To speed up PDHG across diverse OPF scenarios, Loop-OPF learns certain PDHG parameters in a self-supervised manner, without any OPF solution labels. We adopt the deep equilibrium (DEQ) framework for training so that the memory cost does not grow with the number of layers. As the grid topology enters every layer as an input, the same trained Loop-OPF directly adapts to unseen contingencies without retraining. Numerical tests on the IEEE 300-bus and PEGASE 1354-, 2869-, and 9241-bus networks have demonstrated the accuracy and topology adaptivity of the proposed Loop-OPF over competing learning-for-OPF methods.

candidates.title: TrojanMaxxing: One-shotting VLM Backdoors with Weight-Space Programming
candidates.abstract: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can reason directly about the weights of other neural networks. Given only a natural-language objective, an LLM can inspect a model's weights, understand what they compute, and edit them directly without gradient-based optimization. This capability, termed weight-space programming (WSP), has been used to improve model performance on math reasoning, medical QA and other benchmarks. We propose TrojanMaxxing, a novel strategy to backdoor vision-language models (VLMs), by reframing it as a WSP task. We use Claude Opus 5.5 and Mythos 5.2 agents to backdoor VLMs without any optimization or training methods. The agents inspect the model weights, apply targeted edits, and co-design an imperceptible visual trigger that activates the backdoor. We then study the agents' strategies and present a thorough evaluation of the trojaned models on various benchmark datasets. TrojanMaxxing achieves attack success rates of 93%-100% on content moderation and 78%-100% on OCR while maintaining clean accuracy. Perhaps most consequentially, we show that injecting backdoors in a training-free manner is possible by simply, "asking an agent to do it".

candidates.title: Writing Weights or Training Them? Spatial Reasoning through Weight-Space Programming and Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract: Weight-space programming lets a language model inspect and edit another model's weights, offering an alternative to gradient-based adaptation. We evaluated both approaches using Qwen3.5-0.8B on a fixed reference-frame task (128 items), StepGame (200 items), and two untrained distance-comparison tasks. With thinking enabled, the public patch (p50c) raised mean accuracy from 0.0% to 22.1% on the reference-frame task and from 19.2% to 33.7% on StepGame across three sampling seeds. Randomly permuting its weight change removed the gain. Further closed-form edits did not improve on p50c, whereas a rank-1 LoRA adapter trained on worked solutions reached 100% and 98.8%, respectively, with 0.09% trainable parameters. Removing the worked solutions from supervision prevented the adapter from passing the learning gate. The trained adapters reached 82% accuracy on unseen StepGame sentence templates, 42% on held-out difficulty levels 6-10 after training on levels 1-5, and 33-50% on unseen heading-answer combinations. Their target gains coincided with a sharp decline on the distance tasks: accuracy fell from 94% and 92% under p50c to 0-2%, and their outputs applied the StepGame solution template to distance questions. With thinking disabled and reasoning requested in the visible answer, the base model also solved the distance tasks while remaining weak on the target tasks. The comparison reveals a trade-off between improving spatial task performance and preserving neighbouring skills: the public edit restored completion while preserving distance performance, whereas supervised adaptation produced much larger target gains together with interference across tasks.

candidates.title: Weight-space programming and mechanistic interpretability for model editing in particle physics
candidates.abstract: We demonstrate that weight-space programming and edits guided by sparse autoencoders can remove unwanted aspects of a particle-physics foundation model through direct edits to its weights. In a foundation model trained on jets, we observe that adding a single soft neutral particle causes large changes in jet classification, violating infrared safety. We locate the responsible attention heads with mechanistic analysis and trace the flaw's origin to pretraining on datasets with different reconstruction thresholds. We then propose two targeted approaches to repair the flaw: by removing three latent directions identified with sparse autoencoders, and by letting language-model agents edit the weights directly, without gradients and with only 50 queries to the model. Both their edits individually remove almost the entire flaw and leave the rest of the model's response nearly unchanged. Compared to fine-tuning, both methods change far fewer parameters. Although built only on $W$ and QCD jets, the edits carry over to all signal classes, the pretrained generator, and a newly trained regression head.

candidates.title: A Learned Cost Model-based Cross-engine Optimizer for SQL Workloads
candidates.abstract: Lakehouse systems enable the same data to be queried with multiple execution engines. However, selecting the engine best suited to run a SQL query still requires a priori knowledge of the query computational requirements and an engine capability, a complex and manual task that only becomes more difficult with the emergence of new engines and workloads. In this paper, we address this limitation by proposing a cross-engine optimizer that can automate engine selection for diverse SQL queries through a learned cost model. Optimized with hints, a query plan is used for query cost prediction and routing. Cost prediction is formulated as a multi-task learning problem, and multiple predictor heads, corresponding to different engines and provisionings, are used in the model architecture. This eliminates the need to train engine-specific models and allows the flexible addition of new engines at a minimal fine-tuning cost. Results on various databases and engines show that using a query optimized logical plan for cost estimation decreases the average Q-error by even 12.6% over using unoptimized plans as input. Moreover, the proposed cross-engine optimizer reduces the total workload runtime by up to 25.2% in a zero-shot setting and 30.4% in a few-shot setting when compared to random routing.

candidates.title: Can Large Language Models Be Query Optimizer for Relational Databases?
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data
candidates.abstract: Query optimization is a complex planning and decision-making problem within the exponentially growing plan space in database management systems (DBMS). Traditional optimization techniques have been extensively studied over decades, leaving limited room for further improvement along this track. Recent developments of Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated their potential in solving complex planning and decision-making problems, such as arithmetic and programmatic tasks. In this paper, we try to explore the potential of LLMs in handling query optimization and propose a tentative LLM-based query optimizer dubbed LLM-QO, established on PostgreSQL's execution engine. In LLM-QO, we formulate query optimization in an autoregressive fashion which directly generates the execution plan without explicit plan enumeration. To investigate the essential input of LLM-QO, we design a customized data recipe named QInstruct to collect the training data from various optimizers and serialize the database's meta data, queries and corresponding plans into a textual format. Based on QInstruct, we implement a two-stage fine-tuning pipeline, Query Instruction Tuning (QIT) and Query Direct Preference Optimization (QDPO), to empower the capability of general-purpose LLMs in handling query optimization. In our experiments, LLM-QO can generate valid and high-quality plans and consistently outperforms both traditional and learned optimizers on three query workloads. Our findings verify that LLMs can be derived as query optimizers where generalization, efficiency and adaptivity deserve further research efforts.

candidates.title: Learned Offline Query Planning via Bayesian Optimization
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data
candidates.abstract: Analytics database workloads often contain queries that are executed repeatedly. Existing optimization techniques generally prioritize keeping optimization cost low, normally well below the time it takes to execute a single instance of a query. If a given query is going to be executed thousands of times, could it be worth investing significantly more optimization time? In contrast to traditional online query optimizers, we propose an offline query optimizer that searches a wide variety of plans and incorporates query execution as a primitive. Our offline query optimizer combines variational auto-encoders with Bayesian optimization to find optimized plans for a given query. We compare our technique to the optimal plans possible with PostgreSQL and recent RL-based systems over several datasets, and show that our technique finds faster query plans.

candidates.title: Learned Query Optimizer in Alibaba MaxCompute: Challenges, Analysis, and Solutions
candidates.venue: ACM SIGMOD International Conference on Management of Data (SIGMOD)
candidates.abstract: Existing learned query optimizers remain ill-suited to modern distributed, multi-tenant data warehouses due to idealized modeling assumptions and design choices. Using Alibaba's MaxCompute as a representative, we surface four fundamental, system-agnostic challenges for any deployable learned query optimizer: 1) highly dynamic execution environments that induce large variance in plan costs; 2) potential absence of input statistics needed for cost estimation; 3) infeasibility of conventional model refinement; and 4) uncertain benefits across different workloads. These challenges expose a deep mismatch between theoretical advances and production realities and demand a principled, deployment-first redesign of learned optimizers. To bridge this gap, we present LOAM, a one-stop learned query optimization framework for MaxCompute. Its design principles and techniques generalize and are readily adaptable to similar systems. Architecturally, LOAM introduces a statistics-free plan encoding that leverages operator semantics and historical executions to infer details about data distributions and explicitly encodes the execution environments of training queries to learn their impacts on plan costs. For online queries with unknown environments at prediction time, LOAM provides a theoretical bound on the achievable performance and a practical strategy to smooth the environmental impacts on cost estimations. For system operating, LOAM integrates domain adaptation techniques into training to generalize effectively to online query plans without requiring conventional refinement. Additionally, LOAM includes a lightweight project selector to prioritize high-benefit deployment projects. LOAM has seen up to 30% CPU cost savings over MaxCompute's native query optimizer on production workloads, which could translate to substantial real-world resource savings.

candidates.title: JOB-Complex: A Challenging Benchmark for Traditional & Learned Query Optimization
candidates.abstract: Query optimization is a fundamental task in database systems that is crucial to providing high performance. To evaluate learned and traditional optimizer's performance, several benchmarks, such as the widely used JOB benchmark, are used. However, in this paper, we argue that existing benchmarks are inherently limited, as they do not reflect many real-world properties of query optimization, thus overstating the performance of both traditional and learned optimizers. In fact, simple but realistic properties, such as joins over string columns or complex filter predicates, can drastically reduce the performance of existing query optimizers. Thus, we introduce JOB-Complex, a new benchmark designed to challenge traditional and learned query optimizers by reflecting real-world complexity. Overall, JOB-Complex contains 30 SQL queries and comes together with a plan-selection benchmark containing nearly 6000 execution plans, making it a valuable resource to evaluate the performance of query optimizers and cost models in real-world scenarios. In our evaluation, we show that traditional and learned cost models struggle to achieve high performance on JOB-Complex, providing a runtime of up to 11x slower compared to the optimal plans.

candidates.title: LLM4Hint: Leveraging Large Language Models for Hint Recommendation in Offline Query Optimization
candidates.venue: IEEE International Conference on Data Engineering (ICDE)
candidates.abstract: Query optimization is essential for efficient SQL query execution in DBMS, and remains attractive over time due to the growth of data volumes and advances in hardware. Existing traditional optimizers struggle with the cumbersome hand-tuning required for complex workloads, and the learning-based methods face limitations in ensuring generalization. With the great success of Large Language Model (LLM) across diverse downstream tasks, this paper explores how LLMs can be incorporated to enhance the generalization of learned optimizers. Though promising, such an incorporation still presents challenges, mainly including high model inference latency, and the substantial fine-tuning cost and suboptimal performance due to inherent discrepancy between the token sequences in LLM and structured SQL execution plans with rich numerical features. In this paper, we focus on recurring queries in offline optimization to alleviate the issue of high inference latency, and propose \textbf{LLM4Hint} that leverages moderate-sized backbone LLMs to recommend query optimization hints. LLM4Hint achieves the goals through: (i) integrating a lightweight model to produce a soft prompt, which captures the data distribution in DBMS and the SQL predicates to provide sufficient optimization features while simultaneously reducing the context length fed to the LLM, (ii) devising a query rewriting strategy using a larger commercial LLM, so as to simplify SQL semantics for the backbone LLM and reduce fine-tuning costs, and (iii) introducing an explicit matching prompt to facilitate alignment between the LLM and the lightweight model, which can accelerate convergence of the combined model. Experiments show that LLM4Hint, by leveraging the LLM's stronger capability to understand the query statement, can outperform the state-of-the-art learned optimizers in terms of both effectiveness and generalization.

candidates.title: Shielded Reinforcement Learning for Query Optimization: A Formally Verified Framework for Adversarial Robustness in DBMS
candidates.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
candidates.abstract: We present a formally verified framework for Reinforcement Learning-based Query Optimization in Database Management Systems (DBMS) under adversarial workload manipulation. Modern learned optimizers improve performance but introduce a critical vulnerability: susceptibility to cardinality estimation poisoning, which can lead to catastrophic execution plans, including memory overflow (OOM), severe latency degradation, and system instability. To address this, we introduce a Shielded Reinforcement Learning architecture that constrains a learned policy through a formally defined safety layer. The system is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP), together with an abstracted finite-state representation connected via an $\varepsilon_{model}$-bounded probabilistic simulation relation. This abstraction quantifies divergence between physical and modeled transition dynamics using Total Variation distance. A key contribution is a certified fallback mechanism, representing a deterministic and statically verified optimizer path that guarantees bounded memory consumption under all execution traces. On top of this, we design an O(1)-complexity runtime shield that filters policy actions using a precomputed safety relation over a product automaton. We prove a probabilistic safety bound over a finite horizon $T$, showing that the probability of entering an unsafe state is upper-bounded by $T \cdot \varepsilon_{model}$. The proof relies on conditional expectation bounds and union-type arguments over bounded deviation events. Empirical evaluation on TPC-H workloads demonstrates that the proposed framework eliminates OOM failures under adversarial conditions while maintaining competitive latency compared to both classical optimizers (System R-style) and unshielded RL-based approaches. Additional analysis highlights the trade-off between abstraction granularity, synthesis cost, and model fidelity. Overall, this work bridges formal methods and learned database systems, providing a practically deployable yet mathematically grounded safety layer for reinforcement learning-based query optimization in adversarial environments.

candidates.title: E-LQO: A Comprehensive Energy Evaluation Framework for Learned Query Optimization
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data
candidates.abstract: Learned Query Optimization (LQO) has emerged as a promising paradigm for improving database performance, with reported speedups of 2× to over 10× on standard benchmarks. Existing evaluations, however, remain largely latency-centric and leave the energy debt from data collection, model training, and online inference less visible. This paper presents E-LQO, the first comprehensive framework for evaluating energy consumption across the complete LQO lifecycle: data collection or preparation, model training, model inference, and plan execution. We formalize two domain-specific metrics— Energy Return on Investment (EROI) and Energy Payback Time (EPT)—to quantify both per-cycle efficiency and the amortization horizon of learned optimizers. Across seven LQO methods on fixed-scale JOB and on TPC-H/TPC-DS up to 100 GB, we find that lifecycle energy is governed less by whether an optimizer is learned than by how it obtains supervision. Execution-based systems buy plan quality through active exploration and carry a large upfront energy debt; passive/log-driven systems can repay much faster with reusable logs or labels, but this advantage depends on incremental-cost accounting and often comes with weaker latency gains on light workloads. We further show that total online inference energy, including candidate-plan generation, enables symmetric accounting, and that roughly 50% template coverage is the energy-optimal exploration region for the execution-based methods we study. E-LQO provides practitioners with actionable guidance for energy-conscious deployment decisions and exposes optimization opportunities for sustainable learned query optimization.

candidates.title: Simple Adaptive Query Processing vs. Learned Query Optimizers: Observations and Analysis
candidates.abstract: There have been many decades of work on optimizing query processing in database management systems. Recently, modern machine learning (ML), and specifically reinforcement learning (RL), have gained increased attention as a means to develop a query optimizer (QO). In this work, we take a closer look at two recent RL-based QO methods to better understand their behavior. We find that these RL-based methods do not generalize as well as it seems at first glance. Thus, we ask a simple question: How do RL-based QOs compare to a simple, modern, adaptive query processing approach? To answer this question, we chose two simple adaptive query processing techniques and implemented them in PostgreSQL. The first adapts an individual join operation on-the-fly and switches between a Nested Loop Join algorithm and a Hash Join algorithm to avoid sub-optimal join algorithm decisions. The second is a technique called Lookahead Information Passing (LIP), in which adaptive semijoin techniques are used to make a pipeline of join operations execute efficiently. To our surprise, we find that this simple adaptive query processing approach is not only competitive to these RL-based approaches but, in some cases, outperforms the RL-based approaches. The adaptive approach is also appealing because it does not require an expensive training step, and it is fully interpretable compared to the RL-based QO approaches. Further, the adaptive method works across complex query constructs that RL-based QO methods currently cannot optimize.

candidates.title: Learned Cost Models for Query Optimization: From Batch to Streaming Systems
candidates.abstract: Learned cost models (LCMs) have recently gained traction as a promising alternative to traditional cost estimation techniques in data management, offering improved accuracy by capturing complex interactions between queries, data, and runtime behavior. While initially developed for batch systems, LCMs are now increasingly applied to stream processing as well, where real-time demands pose new challenges. This tutorial presents the first unified overview of LCMs across both batch and stream processing systems, examining their role as essential components in modern query optimizers. We explore key aspects of LCM design—including input representations and model architectures—and highlight how these models deal with query optimization tasks.

candidates.title: Adaptive query optimization using reinforcement learning for dynamic cloud database workloads: A review
candidates.venue: International Journal of Computing Programming and Database Management
candidates.abstract: The optimization of queries is one of the most crucial and complex tasks in a DBMS because the join order, access path, physical operator and choice of resources could vary by orders of magnitude in terms of execution performance. The traditional cost-based query optimizers use hand-crafted cost models, static statistics, heuristics for search, and cardinality estimates. Though these mechanisms have come a long way, they also rely on assumptions that are getting tougher in the context of cloud database workloads that are bursty, dynamic on data distribution, dynamically scalable, multi-tenant, heterogeneous, and volatile on resource pricing. Another alternative is when optimization policies are learned from the execution feedback and/or adapt to the workload behaviour learned from past observations, known as reinforcement learning (RL). This paper discusses the development of the conventional cost-based optimization, adaptive query processing, learned cost models, online query optimization, workload-aware tuning and deep reinforcement learning. Comparative analysis of some representative systems such as SkinnerDB, Neo, QTune, Bao, Balsa, CDBTune+, QueryFormer, Lero, Lemo, ADWTune, RankPQO and adaptive parametric optimizers. State representation, safe exploration, workload drift, training cost, reward design, transferability, explainability and integration with existing optimizers are the main challenges identified during the review that restrict the production deployment. A closed loop system is suggested for a reference architecture that includes workload monitoring, a representation of the query plan, drift detection, an adaptive RL policy, safety constraints, and continuous feedback. The review finds that practical cloud query optimization will probably follow the trajectory towards a hybrid model where traditional query optimizers give safe plans and learning components will continually rank, correct and reconfigure plans based on varying workload and infrastructure.

candidates.title: Adaptive and Learned Query Optimization: Techniques, Architectures, and Emerging Trends
candidates.venue: Journal of Informatics and Web Engineering
candidates.abstract: As databases continue to grow and complexity there is an urgent need to achieve more efficient and faster query processing. This paper presents a technical review of methods that work towards optimization of various types of queries. It progresses by focusing on basic approaches like rules-based optimization and cost-based optimization. Based on this basis, the paper presents a synthesized reference architecture for adaptive and learned query optimizers as a generic framework derived from prior system. It explains on how the classical optimizer components can be enhanced through runtime monitoring integration and feedback mechanisms. From this perspective, it becomes possible to explain how learning modules and execution feedback should be added to the standard optimization pipelines instead of requiring any revolutionary changes in the current database systems. Next, various Adaptive Query Processing (AQP) approaches are reviewed to highlight their strengths and limitations. A fundamental aspect to consider with respect to decision-making process is covered in how effective these methods are from a re-optimization point of view, as well as with adaptive operators. The final section discussed the emerging trends in this field, including some current developments and what is expected to come regarding query optimization alongside machine learning integration, and distributed queries handling advancement issues. By synthesizing insights from existing literature, this review equips researchers with a robust understanding of the current state and future potential of query optimization and adaptive processing techniques.

candidates.title: DLLO:A Learned Join Query Optimizer for Data Lake
RELOAD: A Robust and Efficient Learned Query Optimizer for Database Systems
candidates.abstract: Recent advances in query optimization have shifted from traditional rule-based and cost-based techniques towards machine learning-driven approaches. Among these, reinforcement learning (RL) has attracted significant attention due to its ability to optimize long-term performance by learning policies over query planning. However, existing RL-based query optimizers often exhibit unstable performance at the level of individual queries, including severe performance regressions, and require prolonged training to reach the plan quality of expert, cost-based optimizers. These shortcomings make learned query optimizers difficult to deploy in practice and remain a major barrier to their adoption in production database systems. To address these challenges, we present RELOAD, a robust and efficient learned query optimizer for database systems. RELOAD focuses on (i) robustness, by minimizing query-level performance regressions and ensuring consistent optimization behavior across executions, and (ii) efficiency, by accelerating convergence to expert-level plan quality. Through extensive experiments on standard benchmarks, including Join Order Benchmark, TPC-DS, and Star Schema Benchmark, RELOAD demonstrates up to 2.4x higher robustness and 3.1x greater efficiency compared to state-of-the-art RL-based query optimization techniques.

candidates.title: How Good are Learned Cost Models, Really? Insights from Query Optimization Tasks
candidates.venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Management of Data
candidates.abstract: Traditionally, query optimizers rely on cost models to choose the best execution plan from several candidates, making precise cost estimates critical for efficient query execution. In recent years, cost models based on machine learning have been proposed to overcome the weaknesses of traditional cost models. While these models have been shown to provide better prediction accuracy, only limited efforts have been made to investigate how well Learned Cost Models (LCMs) actually perform in query optimization and how they affect overall query performance. In this paper, we address this by a systematic study evaluating LCMs on three of the core query optimization tasks: join ordering, access path selection, and physical operator selection . In our study, we compare seven state-of-the-art LCMs to a traditional cost model and, surprisingly, find that the traditional model often still outperforms LCMs in these tasks. We conclude by highlighting major takeaways and recommendations to guide future research toward making LCMs more effective for query optimization.

candidates.title: Delta: A Learned Mixed Cost-based Query Optimization Framework
candidates.abstract: Query optimizer is a crucial module for database management systems. Existing optimizers exhibit two flawed paradigms: (1) cost-based optimizers use dynamic programming with cost models but face search space explosion and heuristic pruning constraints; (2) value-based ones train value networks to enable efficient beam search, but incur higher training costs and lower accuracy. They also lack mechanisms to detect queries where they may perform poorly. To determine more efficient plans, we propose Delta, a mixed cost-based query optimization framework that consists of a compatible query detector and a two-stage planner. Delta first employs a Mahalanobis distancebased detector to preemptively filter out incompatible queries where the planner might perform poorly. For compatible queries, Delta activates its two-stage mixed cost-based planner. Stage I serves as a coarse-grained filter to generate high-quality candidate plans based on the value network via beam search, relaxing precision requirements and narrowing the search space. Stage II employs a fine-grained ranker to determine the best plan from the candidate plans based on a learned cost model. Moreover, to reduce training costs, we reuse and augment the training data from stage I to train the model in stage II. Experimental results on three workloads demonstrate that Delta identifies higher-quality plans, achieving an average 2.34x speedup over PostgreSQL and outperforming the state-of-the-art learned methods by 2.21x.

candidates.title: LIMAO: A Framework for Lifelong Modular Learned Query Optimization
candidates.abstract: Query optimizers are crucial for the performance of database systems. Recently, many learned query optimizers (LQOs) have demonstrated significant performance improvements over traditional optimizers. However, most of them operate under a limited assumption: a static query environment. This limitation prevents them from effectively handling complex, dynamic query environments in real-world scenarios. Extensive retraining can lead to the well-known catastrophic forgetting problem which reduces the LQO generalizability over time. In this paper, we address this limitation and introduce LIMAO (Lifelong Modular Learned Query Optimizer), a framework for lifelong learning of plan cost prediction that can be seamlessly integrated into existing LQOs. LIMAO leverages a modular lifelong learning technique, an attention-based neural network composition architecture, and an efficient training paradigm designed to retain prior knowledge while continuously adapting to new environments. We implement LIMAO in two LQOs, showing that our approach is agnostic to underlying engines. Experimental results show that LIMAO significantly enhances the performance of LQOs, achieving up to a 40% improvement in query execution time and reducing the variance of execution time by up to 60% under dynamic workloads. By leveraging a precise and self-consistent design, LIMAO effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting, ensuring stable and reliable plan quality over time. Compared to Postgres, LIMAO achieves up to a 4× speedup on selected benchmarks, highlighting its practical advantages in real-world query optimization.

candidates.title: LQRS: Runtime-Aware Learned Query Optimization Framework for Spark SQL
candidates.venue: IEEE Transactions on Knowledge and Data Engineering
candidates.abstract: The query optimizer is a fundamental component of database management systems. Recent studies show that learned query optimizers (LQOs) can outperform traditional cost-based query optimizers. However, most LQO methods remain limited to pre-execution optimization: they make decisions before execution based on estimated statistics and cannot benefit from runtime observations revealed during query execution, which may expose further opportunities for improvement. In this paper, we extend learned query optimization from the pre-execution phase into the in-execution phase and realize this idea through LQRS, a runtime-aware learned query optimization framework built on Spark SQL. LQRS leverages the adaptive query execution foundation of Spark SQL to collect runtime feedback and refine decisions for the remaining plan during execution. Specifically, LQRS employs a curriculum reinforcement learning strategy and unifies pre-execution and in-execution optimization within a single decision process, allowing knowledge acquired from runtime feedback to improve pre-execution planning. Furthermore, we design a plug-and-play planner extension based on the extensibility interfaces of Spark SQL, enabling online plan adaptation. Experiments on Spark SQL show that LQRS reduces end-to-end execution time by up to 90% compared with learned query optimizers and re-optimization methods.

candidates.title: Larch: Learned Query Optimization for Semantic Predicates
candidates.abstract: With the advent of Large Language Models (LLMs), many database systems introduced semantic operators that enabled analytical queries over unstructured data (e.g. text, images, videos). Semantic operators typically incur high inference costs and latencies making semantic (AI) SQL queries challenging to apply on large scale datasets. At the same time, their semantic nature leads database engines to treat them as black boxes, making AISQL queries difficult to optimize. In this paper, we introduce Larch, a framework for optimizing the execution of semantic filters in AI SQL queries. Larch was inspired by two key observations: i) the high latency of semantic operators leaves significant room for computationally-heavy runtime optimization techniques, ii) unstructured data are typically accompanied by semantic information in the form of embeddings allowing for efficient semantic comparisons between AI_FILTER prompts and data values. Based on these two key observations, we present two Larch variants: Larch-A2C and Larch-Sel. Larch-A2C encodes arbitrary semantic filters expression tree using an embedding-augmented Gated Graph Neural Network and formulates the filter evaluation order as a Markov decision process. In contrast, Larch-Sel leverages a supervised learning model to predict filter selectivities, subsequently applying dynamic programming to find a near-optimal evaluation order for each input row. Evaluated across diverse real-world datasets and comprehensive synthetic workloads, both Larch variants always outperform existing semantic filter optimization techniques in terms of token usage on every dataset and workload. Our results demonstrate that Larch is robust across diverse workloads across text and image modalities, 6%--30% lower total token costs and 3x--19x lower token costs overhead than Palimpzest and Quest.
